title: A Natural, Though Corrupt, Love of the Lie
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "Of Truth," in The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral by Francis Bacon (1625).
body: WHAT is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer. Certainly there be, that delight in giddiness, and count it a bondage to fix a belief; affecting free-will in thinking, as well as in acting. And though the sects of philosophers of that kind be gone, yet there remain certain discoursing wits, which are of the same veins, though there be not so much blood in them, as was in those of the ancients. But it is not only the difficulty and labor, which men take in finding out of truth, nor again, that when it is found, it imposeth upon men’s thoughts, that doth bring lies in favor; but a natural, though corrupt love, of the lie itself.

One of the later school of the Grecians, examineth the matter, and is at a stand, to think what should be in it, that men should love lies; where neither they make for pleasure, as with poets, nor for advantage, as with the merchant; but for the lie’s sake. But I cannot tell; this same truth, is a naked, and open day-light, that doth not show the masks, and mummeries, and triumphs, of the world, half so stately and daintily as candle-lights. Truth may perhaps come to the price of a pearl, that showeth best by day; but it will not rise to the price of a diamond, or carbuncle, that showeth best in varied lights. A mixture of a lie doth ever add pleasure. Doth any man doubt, that if there were taken out of men’s minds, vain opinions, flattering hopes, false valuations, imaginations as one would, and the like, but it would leave the minds, of a number of men, poor shrunken things, full of melancholy and indisposition, and unpleasing to themselves?

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who asked "What is truth?" and did not wait for an answer?
options: Jesting Pilate
One of the Grecian philosophers
A discoursing wit
The author's father

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author compare truth to, since it shows best by day?
options: A pearl
A candle
A diamond
A mask

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the author compare to something that "showeth best in varied lights"?
options: A diamond, or carbuncle
A pearl
The sun
A candle-light

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what puzzled one of the later Grecian philosophers?
options: Why men should love lies even without gain from them
Why truth is so hard to find
Why poets tell so many lies
Why merchants are dishonest

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say truth is like daylight rather than candle-light?
options: Truth shows things plainly, without the flattering glow that makes them look better than they are
Truth is only visible at certain times of day
Truth is duller and less interesting than a lie
Truth requires artificial light to be seen clearly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say removing vain opinions and false hopes would leave minds "poor shrunken things"?
options: People rely on comforting illusions to feel content with themselves
People need truth to be physically healthy
People cannot think at all without false beliefs
People would become wealthier without such illusions

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author distinguish the ancient philosophical sects from the "discoursing wits" who remain?
options: To suggest the modern skeptics are a weaker version of the ancient philosophers
To argue that modern philosophers are more honest than ancient ones
To claim the ancient sects were entirely forgotten
To show that both groups agreed completely

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: People are drawn to comforting lies even though truth alone is the highest good
Truth is easy to find once a person looks for it
Lies are always told for pleasure or profit
Ancient philosophers were wiser than anyone since

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the author suggest by noting that lies are loved neither for pleasure, as with poets, nor for advantage, as with merchants?
options: Ordinary people's love of lies is different from lying for art or profit — it is loved for its own sake
Poets and merchants never actually lie
Only poets and merchants are capable of loving a lie
Lies told for pleasure are more harmful than lies told for profit

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that some people "delight in giddiness" rather than fixing a belief?
options: They enjoy uncertainty and constantly shifting opinions
They enjoy dancing and celebration
They become dizzy when they think too hard
They prefer silence to conversation

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the philosophers described believe about fixing a belief?
options: They thought it was a kind of bondage
They thought it was the highest form of freedom
They thought it was impossible to avoid
They thought only the young should attempt it

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does a mixture of a lie always do, according to the author?
options: It adds pleasure
It removes all pleasure
It always causes harm
It has no effect at all

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what kind of love does the author say people have for lies?
options: A natural, though corrupt, love
A love learned only from poets
A love shared by no one at all
A love reserved only for merchants

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the author list as commonly filling men's minds?
options: Vain opinions, flattering hopes, and false valuations
Ancient philosophical texts
Fear of the Grecian school
Memories of candle-light

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author mention that certain philosophers "affect free-will in thinking, as well as in acting"?
options: To compare their resistance to fixed belief with a broader resistance to any constraint
To argue that free will does not exist
To praise them for their consistency
To explain why they became merchants

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the Grecian philosopher's puzzlement described in the passage?
options: He could not explain why people would love lies with nothing to gain from them
He believed all lies were told for profit
He argued that truth was worthless
He concluded that poets never lied

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the modern "discoursing wits" have not so much "blood" in them as the ancients?
options: They have less conviction and vigor in their views
They are physically weaker and often ill
They are younger than the ancient philosophers were
They write in a paler shade of ink
